entry.title: Pandas is a Relational Algebra Library: Foundations, Operations, and Beyond

link.title: Pandas is a Relational Algebra Library: Foundations, Operations, and Beyond

entry.content:
Pandas is a Relational Algebra Library

Understanding Python DataFrames Through Classical Database Theory

A Comparative Exploration Based on Silberschatz, Korth, and Sudarshan (Chapter 2)

Introduction: The Mathematical Backbone of Data Manipulation

Is Pandas merely a sprawling utility belt of hundreds of disconnected methods, or does it rest on a formal mathematical foundation?

The Short Answer: Not quite. You can perform a surprisingly large portion of data manipulation in Pandas using relational algebra, but relational algebra alone is not enough to cover everything Pandas can do.

Think of relational algebra as the mathematical foundation of structured data manipulation.

When data practitioners learn Pandas purely by memorizing function signatures (.loc, .merge, .apply, .pivot), the library often feels arbitrary and overwhelming. However, once you view Pandas through the lens of formal database systems—specifically Chapter 2 of Database System Concepts by Silberschatz, Korth, and Sudarshan (db-book.com Chapter 2 Slides)—the core design becomes coherent, elegant, and predictable.

In this post, we establish a direct bridge between classical relational algebra and the Pandas API, analyze where Pandas transcends classical relational theory, and examine why reasoning algebraically makes you a vastly more effective engineer.

1. Classical Foundations: Relations vs. DataFrames

Before inspecting operations, we must examine the underlying data structures.

In classical database theory (Silberschatz et al., Section 2.1–2.2):

  • A Relation Schema $R = (A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n)$ is a named set of attributes where each attribute $A_i$ draws values from a defined domain $\text{dom}(A_i)$.
  • A Relation Instance $r(R)$ is a formal mathematical relation—a finite set of unordered tuples: \(r(R) \subseteq \text{dom}(A_1) \times \text{dom}(A_2) \times \dots \times \text{dom}(A_n)\)
  • Because a relation is a set, duplicate tuples cannot exist, and tuple order is strictly undefined.

How a Pandas DataFrame Extends the Relation

A Pandas DataFrame implements a relation-like 2D structure, but makes crucial departures from pure set theory:

  1. Explicit Row Coordinates (Index): Unlike a mathematical set where tuples have no order or identity, a DataFrame has an ordered axis index (df.index). This allows 0-indexed positional lookups (iloc) and label-based slicing (loc).
  2. Duplicate Semantics (Multisets / Bags): Relational algebra forbids identical tuples. Pandas permits duplicate rows and even duplicate column labels unless explicitly deduplicated with .drop_duplicates().
  3. Column Order Preservation: Relational attributes are an unordered set ${A_1, \dots, A_n}$. In Pandas, columns form an ordered sequence, allowing positional column indexing (df.iloc[:, 0]).

2. What Relational Algebra Covers: The Classical Toolkit in Pandas

Classical relational algebra defines a collection of closed operations that accept one or more relations as input and yield a new relation as output. Silberschatz et al. categorize these into fundamental operations and derived operations.

The table below summarizes how the classical operations map directly to Pandas:

Operation Mathematical Notation What You Can Do Pandas Implementation
Selection $\sigma_p(r)$ Filter rows satisfying predicate $p$ df[df['col'] > val] or df.query('col > val')
Projection $\Pi_{A_1, \dots, A_k}(r)$ Select and retain specific columns df[['col1', 'col2']]
Union $r \cup s$ Combine rows from two compatible datasets pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True)
Set Difference $r - s$ Find tuples in $r$ that do not appear in $s$ df1[~df1.isin(df2).all(axis=1)]
Cartesian Product $r \times s$ Generate all pairwise tuple combinations df1.merge(df2, how='cross')
Rename $\rho_{S(B_1, \dots, B_n)}(r)$ Rename relation attributes or the relation itself df.rename(columns={'old': 'new'})
Natural / Theta Join $r \bowtie s$ / $r \bowtie_\theta s$ Combine related datasets on matching keys pd.merge(df1, df2, on='key')
Set Intersection $r \cap s$ Find tuples appearing in both relations pd.merge(df1, df2, how='inner')

With these operations alone, you can express an enormous portion of data extraction and transformation logic. Let us inspect each primitive in detail.

2.1 Selection ($\sigma$)

The Selection operator acts as a horizontal filter, selecting tuples that satisfy a boolean predicate $p$:

\[\sigma_p(r) = \{ t \mid t \in r \text{ and } p(t) = \text{True} \}\]

In Pandas, selection is expressed via boolean vector masking or the declarative .query() method:

# Relational Algebra: \sigma_{GPA > 3.5 \land Department = 'CS'}(Student)

# Approach 1: Boolean indexing (loc)
cs_honors = df.loc[(df["GPA"] > 3.5) & (df["Department"] == "CS")]

# Approach 2: Declarative query string
cs_honors = df.query("GPA > 3.5 and Department == 'CS'")

2.2 Projection ($\Pi$)

The Projection operator performs vertical subsetting, keeping specified columns and discarding all others:

\[\Pi_{A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k}(r) = \{ t[A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k] \mid t \in r \}\]

In pure relational algebra, projection automatically eliminates duplicate rows because the output must remain a mathematical set. In Pandas, duplicates are preserved by default:

# Relational Algebra: \Pi_{Name, GPA}(Student)

# Pandas preserves duplicates (bag semantics)
student_summary = df[["Name", "GPA"]]

# Pure Relational Algebra equivalent (set semantics)
student_summary_distinct = df[["Name", "GPA"]].drop_duplicates()

2.3 Union ($r \cup s$) and Set Difference ($r - s$)

Both operations require union-compatibility: the relations must possess identical arity (same number of attributes) and compatible domains.

  • Union ($r \cup s$): \(r \cup s = \{ t \mid t \in r \lor t \in s \}\)

    # Pandas: Concatenate along rows and eliminate duplicates
union_df = pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True).drop_duplicates()

  • Set Difference ($r - s$): \(r - s = \{ t \mid t \in r \land t \notin s \}\) In Pandas, set difference across all columns is commonly implemented via an anti-join:

    diff_df = pd.merge(df1, df2, how="left", indicator=True).query(
    '_merge == "left_only"'
).drop(columns="_merge")

2.4 Cartesian Product ($r \times s$) & Joins ($r \bowtie s$)

The Cartesian Product combines every tuple of relation $r$ with every tuple of relation $s$:

\[r \times s = \{ t \parallel q \mid t \in r \land q \in s \}\]

When $r$ has $n_1$ tuples and $s$ has $n_2$ tuples, the result contains $n_1 \times n_2$ tuples. While rarely used directly in production due to combinatorial explosion, it forms the theoretical foundation of all joins:

\[\text{Theta Join: } r \bowtie_\theta s = \sigma_\theta(r \times s)\] \[\text{Natural Join: } r \bowtie s = \Pi_{R \cup S}\big(\sigma_{r.A_1 = s.A_1 \land \dots \land r.A_k = s.A_k}(r \times s)\big)\]

In Pandas:

# Cartesian Product (r \times s)
cartesian = df1.merge(df2, how="cross")

# Equi-Join / Natural Join (r \bowtie s)
natural_join = pd.merge(student_df, department_df, on="dept_id")

# Outer Joins (Preserving dangling tuples with nulls)
left_outer = pd.merge(student_df, department_df, on="dept_id", how="left")
full_outer = pd.merge(student_df, department_df, on="dept_id", how="outer")

2.5 Rename ($\rho$)

In complex queries, disambiguating attribute names or referencing the same relation multiple times (such as in self-joins) requires the Rename operator:

\[\rho_{S(B_1, B_2, \dots, B_n)}(r)\]

In Pandas:

# Rename specific columns
renamed_df = df.rename(columns={"salary": "compensation", "dept": "department"})

# Rename entire column axis
renamed_df = df.set_axis(["ID", "Name", "Score"], axis=1)

3. What Else Does Pandas Offer? (Beyond Classical Relational Algebra)

While classical relational algebra provides a complete foundation for basic retrieval, modern data science and analytical engineering require transformations that either violate pure set semantics or operate in the geometric/temporal domain.

Pandas was created by Wes McKinney in quantitative finance, where time series alignment, matrix computations, and wide-format data manipulation are essential. Consequently, Pandas includes powerful capabilities outside the classical algebra:

Pandas Capability API Example Why It Lies Beyond Classical Relational Algebra
Aggregation & Grouping df.groupby("dept")["salary"].mean() Requires partitioned reduction over multisets (Extended Relational Algebra)
Sorting df.sort_values("timestamp") Classical relations are strictly unordered sets; order has no algebraic meaning
Statistical Analysis df.corr(), df.describe() Matrix-level mathematical summarization over continuous numeric domains
Missing Data Handling df.fillna(), df.interpolate() Programmatic imputation and numerical reconstruction of incomplete observations
Time Series Resampling df.resample("1D").mean() Domain-specific calendar awareness, frequency conversion, and temporal binning
Window & Rolling Operations df["val"].rolling(window=7).mean() Positional, order-dependent sequence convolution
Reshaping (Pivoting / Melting) df.pivot(...), df.melt(...) Dynamic structural transmutation between data values and schema attribute headers
Vectorized Numerical Arithmetic df["total"] = df["qty"] * df["price"] Element-wise SIMD array broadcasting (linear algebra semantics)

Concrete Example: Grouping & Aggregation

Consider computing the average salary per department:

df.groupby("department")["salary"].mean()

Classical relational algebra (as originally formulated by E. F. Codd in 1970) did not include aggregation. Later extensions—known as Extended Relational Algebra (Silberschatz et al., Section 2.7)—introduced the aggregate operator $\mathcal{G}$ (or $\gamma$):

\[_{\text{department}} \mathcal{G}_{\text{avg}(\text{salary})}(\text{Instructor})\]

However, Pandas takes aggregation much further than $\mathcal{G}$. With .agg(), .transform(), and custom lambda functions, Pandas can compute multi-level descriptive statistics, windowed cumulative aggregates, and expanding statistical moments within a single pipeline.

4. The Tripartite Equivalence: SQL, Relational Algebra, and Pandas

One of the most enlightening realizations in computer science is that declarative SQL, mathematical Relational Algebra, and procedural Pandas code are often three distinct syntaxes expressing the exact same abstract semantic plan.

Consider this simple query:

“Retrieve the names and GPAs of all students whose GPA exceeds 16.”

                             [ Conceptual Intent ]
                   "Filter students with GPA > 16, keep Name & GPA"
                                      │
         ┌────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                            ▼                            ▼
   [ Relational Algebra ]           [ SQL ]                     [ Pandas ]
 \Pi_{Name, GPA}(                SELECT Name, GPA             df.loc[
   \sigma_{GPA > 16}(Student)    FROM Student                   df["GPA"] > 16,
 )                               WHERE GPA > 16;                ["Name", "GPA"]
                                                              ]

The Three Representations:

  1. SQL (Declarative Query): 
    SELECT name, GPA
FROM Student
WHERE GPA > 16;
  2. Relational Algebra (Formal Expression): \(\Pi_{\text{name}, \text{GPA}}\big(\sigma_{\text{GPA} > 16}(\text{Student})\big)\)
  3. Pandas (DataFrame Expression): 
    df.loc[df["GPA"] > 16, ["name", "GPA"]]

Why Database Engines Care: Query Optimization

Database engines (PostgreSQL, SQLite, Snowflake) do not execute SQL text directly. They first parse the SQL into a Relational Algebra Expression Tree. Because relational algebra obeys formal algebraic equivalence rules, the query optimizer can rewrite the tree into an execution plan that runs orders of magnitude faster.

Practical Example: Predicate Pushdown

Suppose we want to find instructors in the Computer Science department who earn more than $80,000:

\[\text{Initial Plan: } \Pi_{\text{name}}\Big(\sigma_{\text{salary} > 80000 \land \text{dept\_name} = \text{'CS'}}(\text{Instructor} \bowtie \text{Department})\Big)\]

If a naive system executes the join first, it combines millions of rows from both tables before filtering. However, relational algebra guarantees the equivalence:

\[\sigma_{p}(r \bowtie s) \equiv \big(\sigma_p(r)\big) \bowtie s \quad (\text{when predicate } p \text{ references only attributes of } r)\]

The optimizer pushes the selection down:

\[\text{Optimized Plan: } \Pi_{\text{name}}\Big(\big(\sigma_{\text{salary} > 80000 \land \text{dept\_name} = \text{'CS'}}(\text{Instructor})\big) \bowtie \text{Department}\Big)\]

In Pandas, applying this exact mathematical insight manually prevents catastrophic memory overhead:

# Naive approach: Join first (burns RAM), filter second
result = pd.merge(large_instructors, departments, on="dept_id").query(
    "salary > 80000 and dept_name == 'CS'"
)

# Algebraic approach: Pushdown filter first, join smaller subset
filtered_instructors = large_instructors.query("salary > 80000")
result = pd.merge(filtered_instructors, departments.query("dept_name == 'CS'"), on="dept_id")

5. The Bigger Picture: The Ecosystem Hierarchy

Relational algebra is not an isolated academic artifact. It serves as the universal foundation across the modern data stack:

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                  RELATIONAL ALGEBRA                                     |
|                       Mathematical Foundations (Codd 1970)                              |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                             │
                      ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
                      ▼                      ▼                      ▼
               [ Standard SQL ]         [ Pandas ]        [ Distributed Engines ]
            Declarative queries for   In-memory data       Apache Spark, DuckDB,
               RDBMS (Postgres,        manipulation,         Polars LazyFrames,
               SQLite, BigQuery)       Series & Matrix          Trino, Snowflake
Layer System Primary Focus Execution Model
Mathematical Theory Relational Algebra Mathematical abstractions & equivalence laws Theoretical / Symbolic
Declarative Query SQL Standard database queries across tables Declarative (Engine optimizes)
In-Memory Manipulation Pandas Flexible analysis, time series, arrays, cleanup Procedural / Eager
Vectorized DataFrames Polars / DuckDB Relational algebra plans with Arrow memory Lazy evaluation / Pushdown
Distributed Big Data Apache Spark DataFrames Petabyte-scale distributed data processing Catalyst Relational Optimizer

6. Conclusion: Why Learn Relational Algebra Deeply?

Libraries and APIs change constantly. A decade ago, data engineers used R data frames and MapReduce. Today, they write Pandas, Polars, and DuckDB. Tomorrow, new runtimes will emerge.

However:

The underlying algebraic language of structured data remains invariant.

When you learn relational algebra deeply:

  1. You stop memorizing arbitrary functions: Instead of struggling to recall how a specific Pandas method behaves, you recognize that you are simply computing a projection, a theta-join, or an anti-join.
  2. You write performant code instinctively: You immediately spot performance anti-patterns—such as row-wise for loops, unintended Cartesian products, or joins executed before selections.
  3. You transition effortlessly across the data stack: Moving between Pandas, SQL, PySpark, Polars, or DuckDB ceases to be a language barrier, because you are expressing the exact same relational transformations across different syntax wrappers.

Take the time to study classical database theory. Mastering the mathematical foundations will serve you far longer than any single programming library.

References

  1. Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2020). Database System Concepts (7th ed.), Chapter 2: The Relational Model. McGraw-Hill. Slide Deck (PDF).
  2. Codd, E. F. (1970). A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks. Communications of the ACM, 13(6), 377–387.
  3. McKinney, W. (2010). Data Structures for Statistical Computing in Python. In Proceedings of the 9th Python in Science Conference (SciPy 2010), pp. 56–61.
entry.summary: A formal and practical examination of Pandas through the lens of classical Relational Algebra (Silberschatz et al., Chapter 2), mapping fundamental relational operators to Pandas and exploring where DataFrame computing transcends classical theory.

entry.title: Human-Exclusive Information Channels: Cryptographic & Perceptual Obfuscation Against Large Language Models

link.title: Human-Exclusive Information Channels: Cryptographic & Perceptual Obfuscation Against Large Language Models

entry.content:
Human-Exclusive Information Channels

Cryptographic & Perceptual Methods to Hide Public Text from LLMs

A Technical Treatise & Interactive Demonstration on Asymmetric Human-AI Information Delivery

1. The Core Dilemma: Public Accessibility vs. Unconsented AI Ingestion

The modern open web is grounded on a decades-old axiom: if information is public, it must be universally machine-readable. For search engines indexing documents via HTTP GET, this premise fostered open access. However, the rapid proliferation of automated scraping infrastructure for Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training corpora, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) scrapers, and autonomous web-agent workers has radically destabilized this dynamic.

Authors, researchers, domain experts, and privacy-conscious publishers face an asymmetric dilemma:

The Publisher’s Paradox: How can an author distribute text across the public web so that any human reader can read it instantaneously with zero login walls or identity checks, while ensuring that automated scrapers, tokenizer pipelines, and multimodal Vision-Language Models (VLMs) ingest only undecipherable entropy or poison?

Addressing this requires constructing a Human-Exclusive Information Channel (HEIC). In this treatise, we systematically dissect the threat model hierarchy across four distinct tiers of automated extraction—and develop live, verifiable defenses for each.

2. The Threat Hierarchy of Automated Extraction

To design principled defenses, we model the adversarial extractor across four escalating capabilities:

Tier Adversary Type Inspection Vector Extraction Mechanism Defensive Primitive
Tier 1 Raw HTTP Scrapers (curl, GPTBot, CCBot) Static HTTP response body Ingests raw .html, .json, or raw byte streams without JS execution Client-Side Proof-of-Work + WebCrypto
Tier 2 Headless Browser & DOM Scrapers (Playwright, Puppeteer) Rendered DOM tree / Clipboard events Queries DOM elements (innerText, textContent) or fires clipboard copy events Bijective Font Glyph Substitution (cmap)
Tier 3 Tokenizer & Latent Ingestion (BPE, WordPiece) Unicode codepoints & semantic embeddings Chunks UTF-8 byte sequences into integer token IDs $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ Adversarial Subword Splitting & Homoglyphs
Tier 4 Multimodal Vision-Language Models & OCR (GPT-4o, Gemini, Screen Scrapers) Rendered optical viewport Takes static raster screenshots ($H \times W \times 3$) and runs ViT patch recognition Sub-Frame Temporal Multiplexing & Kinetic Parallax

Below, we analyze and simulate each defensive layer interactively.

3. Tier 1 Defenses: Client-Side Proof-of-Work & Asymmetric WebCrypto

3.1 The Static Web Vulnerability & The Computational Tollbooth

To understand how Tier 1 operates, consider the architectural constraint of modern static hosting (such as GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, or AWS S3):

The Static Server Dilemma: In a static deployment, there is no server-side backend (e.g., Python, Node.js, PHP) executing authentication logic per request. The server merely acts as a passive file host. When a visitor requests article.html, the web server streams the raw files across the wire without checking identities.

Under this architecture, automated scrapers (e.g., curl, Python’s requests, or commercial LLM crawlers like GPTBot and CCBot) enjoy a massive structural advantage:

  1. They issue an HTTP GET request.
  2. They receive the plain HTML in $\approx 2\text{–}5\text{ ms}$.
  3. They extract the textual content using simple regex or string parsing with virtually zero CPU overhead ($< 1\text{ ms}$).

Why Naive Client-Side Encryption Fails

If an author attempts to protect their text by encrypting it with a symmetric cipher (such as AES-256) and shipping the decryption key inside their client-side JavaScript bundle (app.js), the protection is trivially bypassed: any scraper developer can simply inspect the script, extract the static key, and decrypt the protected text in milliseconds.

The Solution: The “Proof-of-Work” Computational Tollbooth

Instead of providing the decryption key directly or serving plaintext HTML, the static webpage presents the client with a mathematical challenge (a Proof-of-Work puzzle, derived from Adam Back’s Hashcash [1]).

The static server does not possess or transmit any secret symmetric key. Instead, the document contains an authenticated ciphertext safe and an algorithmic challenge: the visiting browser must expend a small, bounded amount of CPU work to derive the decryption key locally.

3.2 Step-by-Step Execution Lifecycle & Mathematical Mechanics

To implement this without an active backend, the static document bundles a cryptographic challenge package containing the encrypted content alongside public challenge parameters:

\[\mathcal{P}_{\text{package}} = \Big\langle S, \; d, \; \mathbf{iv}, \; C, \; T \Big\rangle\]

where:

  • $S \in {0, 1}^{256}$ is a high-entropy, per-document cryptographic salt.
  • $d \in \mathbb{N}$ is the difficulty target (specifying the required number of leading zero bits).
  • $\mathbf{iv} \in {0, 1}^{96}$ is the standard 12-byte initialization vector for AES-GCM.
  • $C \in {0, 1}^*$ is the ciphertext buffer containing the encrypted text (the hidden article content).
  • $T \in {0, 1}^{128}$ is the 16-byte Poly1305 / GHASH authentication tag verifying data integrity.

Here is the exact mathematical lifecycle executed in the client runtime:

1. Why and How the Salt ($S$) is Incorporated

A common vulnerability in naive Proof-of-Work schemes is susceptibility to precomputation attacks (such as rainbow tables or pre-mined nonces).

  • The Attack Without a Salt: If every page used a fixed challenge (e.g., finding $\eta$ such that $\text{SHA-256}(\eta)$ begins with $d$ zeroes), an adversary could compute the winning nonce $\eta^*$ once offline, store it, and instantly bypass the challenge on every single page across your entire website in $0\text{ ms}$.
  • Generation & Binding of the Salt: During page creation, the author generates a fresh 256-bit cryptographically secure pseudo-random salt: \(S \xleftarrow{\$} \{0, 1\}^{256}\) By prepending this unique salt to every candidate nonce ($S \parallel \eta$), the cryptographic avalanche effect of SHA-256 guarantees that the resulting hash output is completely pseudo-random and independent across different documents. Even a single bit difference in $S$ alters $\approx 50\%$ of the digest bits.
  • Per-Document Cryptographic Isolation: Because every article is provisioned with a distinct salt $S_i$, the winning nonce for Page A is mathematically invalid for Page B: \(\eta^*_{\text{Page } A} \neq \eta^*_{\text{Page } B}\) An automated crawler is strictly forced to run the mining loop independently for every individual URL it attempts to harvest.

2. Client-Side Nonce Search (Proof-of-Work Mining)

Upon receiving $\mathcal{P}_{\text{package}}$, the client’s browser launches an asynchronous JavaScript Web Worker thread that searches for the smallest non-negative integer $\eta \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfying a partial pre-image constraint:

\[\text{Find } \eta^* = \min \left\{ \eta \in \mathbb{N} \;\middle|\; \text{SHA-256}(S \parallel \eta) < \frac{2^{256}}{2^d} \right\}\]

In binary terms, the condition requires that the first $d$ bits of the 256-bit digest are all zeroes:

\[\text{SHA-256}(S \parallel \eta) = \underbrace{00\dots0}_{d \text{ bits}} \, b_{d+1} b_{d+2} \dots b_{256}\]

Because SHA-256 is collision-resistant and behaves as a random oracle, there is no shortcut or algebraic inversion. The expected number of hash evaluations to discover $\eta^*$ is geometrically distributed with mean:

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{Iterations}] = 2^d\]

3. Deterministic Key Derivation via HKDF

Once the browser identifies the valid nonce $\eta^$, it must reconstruct the symmetric AES encryption key $K$. It passes both the salt $S$ and the solved input $S \parallel \eta^$ into the HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF-SHA256, RFC 5869):

\[\text{PRK} = \text{HMAC-SHA256}\big(\text{key} = S, \; \text{data} = S \parallel \eta^*\big)\] \[K = \text{HMAC-SHA256}\big(\text{key} = \text{PRK}, \; \text{info} = \text{"heic-v1-aes-key"} \parallel \text{0x01}\big) \quad \in \{0, 1\}^{256}\]

Notice the mathematical beauty: the static server never stored or transmitted the key $K$. The key exists only as a latent cryptographic coordinate reachable solely by expending $2^d$ computational work.

4. Authenticated Decryption of the Ciphertext ($C$)

With key $K$ reconstructed, the browser invokes the native Web Cryptography API (window.crypto.subtle.decrypt [7]) to perform authenticated decryption:

\[M = \text{AES-256-GCM-Decrypt}_{K}\big(\mathbf{iv}, \; C, \; T\big)\]
  • Integrity Guarantee: If an adversary attempts to guess $\eta$ or passes an incorrect key $K’$, the Galois Hash authentication tag $T$ fails verification: \(\text{AES-256-GCM-Decrypt}_{K'}(\mathbf{iv}, C, T) = \bot \quad (\text{Cryptographic Error})\) Not a single bit of plaintext $M$ is revealed unless the client provides the exact mathematically valid nonce.
  • Ephemeral In-Memory Rendering: When valid, the plaintext $M$ is injected directly into the document DOM. The key $K$ is kept strictly in volatile execution memory and never written to cookies, local storage, or network logs.

End-to-End Architectural Flowchart

The entire challenge-response lifecycle across the static server and client runtime is synthesized below:

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           STATIC SERVER (AWS S3 / GitHub Pages)                         |
|                                                                                         |
|   Static Document Package:                                                              |
|   P = < Salt S, Difficulty d, IV, Ciphertext C, Auth Tag T >                            |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                             │
                                             │  HTTP GET Response (Zero Server Logic)
                                             ▼
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                CLIENT BROWSER (V8 / WebAssembly)                        |
|                                                                                         |
|   [Phase 1: Computational Mining Loop]                                                  |
|   For η = 0, 1, 2, 3, ...                                                               |
|   Compute: H = SHA-256(S ∥ η)                                                           |
|   Condition: Does H have d leading zero bits?                                           |
|              ├─ NO  ──> Increment η and repeat                                          |
|              └─ YES ──> Solution Found: η*                                              |
|                                                                                         |
|   [Phase 2: Cryptographic Key Derivation]                                               |
|   K = HKDF-SHA256( Salt = S, IKM = S ∥ η*, Info = "heic-v1-aes-key" )                   |
|                                                                                         |
|   [Phase 3: Authenticated In-Memory Decryption]                                         |
|   Plaintext M = AES-256-GCM-Decrypt( Key = K, IV, Ciphertext = C, Tag = T )             |
|                                                                                         |
|   [Phase 4: Ephemeral DOM Rendering]                                                     |
|   Inject M into Document Object Model ──> Render to Human Retina                        |
|   Discard Key K from volatile execution memory                                          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

3.3 The Core Mechanism: Economic & Computational Asymmetry

Why does this simple mechanism present an existential barrier to automated LLM scrapers while remaining completely painless for a real human?

The defensive power relies entirely on the asymmetry of scale:

Metric Single Human Reader Automated LLM Crawler Fleet
Target Scale Visiting 1 article to read Scraping $10,000,000+$ pages across the web
Execution Environment Standard web browser (Chrome, Safari, Firefox) Lightweight headless HTTP workers (urllib, aiohttp, Go)
Required Hash Operations $\approx 2^{14} = 16,384\text{ iterations}$ $10^7 \times 2^{14} \approx \mathbf{163.8\text{ Billion iterations}}$
Client Execution Latency $30\text{–}50\text{ ms}$ (in-browser background worker) Thousands of CPU-hours of sustained crunching
Human User Experience Completely imperceptible (faster than human ocular saccade) Economic collapse of the web-scraping business model

The Mathematical Asymmetry Explained

  • For a Human Reader: The human brain’s visual processing threshold is approximately $100\text{–}200\text{ ms}$. Running $16,000$ SHA-256 iterations on a modern laptop or smartphone takes roughly $35\text{ ms}$ in a background Web Worker. By the time the reader’s eye finishes tracking to the first headline, the protected text has already been unlocked and rendered. The user experiences zero perceptible friction.
  • For an LLM Crawler (e.g., Common Crawl, GPTBot): Scrapers rely on scraping thousands of pages per second over low-cost cloud instances with minimal CPU overhead. When confronted with a PoW challenge:
    1. They can no longer use simple HTTP clients: A standard curl or requests.get() script receives only undecipherable AES ciphertext hex chunks.
    2. They must spin up full JavaScript engines: To solve the challenge, the scraper must run a heavyweight browser instance (such as Headless Chromium / Puppeteer), which increases memory consumption from 5 MB to 200 MB per worker thread.
    3. The computational bill explodes: Computing 160 billion SHA-256 operations turns what used to be a free $10/month crawling job into thousands of dollars in cloud electricity and weeks of bottlenecked processing.

Interactive Laboratory 1: Client-Side WebCrypto + PoW Engine

Use the simulator below to test client-side cryptographic key derivation. Adjust the difficulty target and execute the browser miner:

Lab 1: Client-Side Proof-of-Work & AES-256-GCM Engine

Tier 1 Defense
14 bits
Iterations Computed ($\eta$): 0
Derived SHA-256 Digest: 0x00000000...
Client Mining Latency: 0 ms
Economic Asymmetry Disparity
DECRYPTED TEXT BUFFER (ORIGINAL ARTICLE):
0x8F4A2C91E0B73D56A14F98C20E5B71D39A4F62C81E0B73D56A14F98C20E5B71D39A4F62C8... [LOCKED CIPHERTEXT]
Ready to compute. Secret article text is encrypted with AES-256-GCM.

4. Tier 2 Defenses: Bijective Glyph Substitution Ciphers (cmap Permutations)

4.1 Exploiting the Split Between Unicode Semantics and Font Glyphs

Even if a headless browser (e.g., Puppeteer, Playwright) executes JavaScript and evaluates the WebCrypto decryption, it typically extracts text by invoking:

const capturedText = element.innerText; // or element.textContent

This reveals the second architectural vulnerability of digital typography: the decoupling of Unicode semantic codepoints from vector rendering glyphs.

HTML Codepoints (DOM)      OpenType / WOFF2 Font             Human Retina
[ U+0071 ] ("q")  =======> [ Glyph ID 84: Outline of 'T' ] ======> Sees: "T"
[ U+0038 ] ("8")  =======> [ Glyph ID 41: Outline of 'h' ] ======> Sees: "h"
[ U+0023 ] ("#")  =======> [ Glyph ID 29: Outline of 'e' ] ======> Sees: "e"

In standard typography, the OpenType cmap (Character to Glyph Mapping) table provides an identity or standard mapping:

\[\text{Codepoint } U \xrightarrow{\text{cmap}} \text{Glyph Outline } G(U)\]
In a Bijective Glyph Substitution Channel (building upon adversarial typography and glyph perturbation principles [6]), the publisher dynamically generates a session-keyed permutation $\pi \in S_{ \Sigma }$ across the printable character alphabet $\Sigma$. The underlying DOM tree contains exclusively permuted codepoints:
\[c_i = \pi(m_i)\]

Simultaneously, the webpage loads an ephemeral, in-memory .woff2 font file whose internal cmap table is deliberately permuted with the inverse mapping $\pi^{-1}$:

\[\text{Glyph}(\pi(m_i)) = \text{Outline}(m_i)\]

4.2 The Clipboard & DOM Trap

Because modern operating systems copy the raw Unicode codepoints from the DOM rather than rasterizing visual pixels into text:

  1. The human reader looks at the screen and perceives normal, beautiful typography.
  2. An LLM scraper reading the DOM receives a cryptographically scrambled sequence.
  3. If an adversary attempts to highlight, copy, and paste the text into ChatGPT, Claude, or a RAG vector database, the clipboard receives only the cipher stream $c_1 c_2 \dots c_n$.

Interactive Laboratory 2: Live Copy-Paste Trap & Glyph Inspector

Try selecting the highlighted text below with your mouse, copy it (Ctrl+C / Cmd+C), and paste it (Ctrl+V / Cmd+V) into the interactive verification box on the right (or directly into your terminal or an LLM):

Lab 2: Bijective Glyph / DOM Substitution & Clipboard Trap

Tier 2 Defense
Human Viewport (Rendered On Screen)
Modern linguistic models presuppose an invariant correspondence between DOM codepoints and semantic tokens. When we dissect this foundational assumption, biological vision perceives continuous optical geometry, whereas automated scrapers ingest only permuted cryptographic entropy.
Highlight the text above and press copy!
Paste Verification Sandbox (What AI Receives)
Underlying DOM Raw Text: Loading...

5. Tier 3 Defenses: Adversarial BPE Token-Splitting & Latent Collapse

5.1 Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) Foundations

Large Language Models do not process raw text strings directly; they decompose input strings into sequences of discrete subword tokens via greedy merge tables (such as OpenAI’s tiktoken or HuggingFace’s tokenizers).

Let $\mathcal{V}$ be the tokenizer vocabulary and $\mathcal{M}$ be the ranked merge rules. Given a clean word $W = \text{“Reinforcement”}$, a typical BPE tokenizer assigns a single unified token:

\[W \xrightarrow{\text{Tokenize}} [42191]\]

The embedding layer maps this token directly to an informative point in representation space:

\[\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{E}[42191] \in \mathbb{R}^d\]

5.2 Adversarial Unicode Perturbation

As established by Boucher et al. in Bad Characters [2], modern subword tokenizers (BPE, WordPiece) are acutely fragile to imperceptible code-point injections. By injecting zero-width non-printing codepoints—specifically:

  • U+200B (Zero-Width Space)
  • U+200C (Zero-Width Non-Joiner)
  • U+2060 (Word Joiner)

or substituting identical visual glyphs with their Cyrillic or Greek homoglyphs (e.g., Latin 'a' $\rightarrow$ Cyrillic 'а' U+0430, Latin 'o' $\rightarrow$ Cyrillic 'о' U+043E) [4], [5], the human visual perception is invariant:

\[\text{Render}(W) \equiv \text{Render}(W_{\text{adv}})\]

However, the BPE tokenizer cannot merge sequences containing interleaved control characters or non-Latin byte prefixes. The tokenization degenerates into single-character and unknown control tokens:

\[W_{\text{adv}} \xrightarrow{\text{Tokenize}} [49, 99401, 11892, 99401, 239, 981, \dots]\]

5.3 Mathematical Impact on Transformer Self-Attention

This injection induces two distinct catastrophic failure modes in LLM inference and RAG vector search:

  1. Quadratic Sequence Inflation: The input token count explodes by a factor of $3\times\text{ to }6\times$, diluting the attention budget $\text{Softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)$ across uninformative separator tokens.
  2. Cosine Distance Degradation: In vector embedding spaces (e.g., text-embedding-3-large, BGE-M3), the similarity between the clean document vector $\mathbf{v}$ and the perturbed vector $\mathbf{v}_{\text{adv}}$ collapses:
\[\cos(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}_{\text{adv}}) = \frac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{\text{adv}}}{\|\mathbf{v}\| \|\mathbf{v}_{\text{adv}}\|} \longrightarrow 0.05 \text{ -- } 0.25\]

This ensures that semantic search queries in RAG systems fail to retrieve the protected passage entirely.

Interactive Laboratory 3: Adversarial BPE Tokenizer Sandbox

Type any sentence into the prompt box and adjust the perturbation slider to observe in real-time how the token stream shatters into disconnected subword IDs while human legibility remains intact:

Cryptographic protocols dissect and obfuscate semantic representations against automated neural ingestion.
LLM BPE TOKEN SEQUENCE BREAKDOWN:

6. Tier 4 Defenses: Breaking the Screenshot Barrier (Anti-Multimodal Vision & OCR)

6.1 The Multimodal Challenge: Optical Character Recognition & VLMs

The most sophisticated threat to human-exclusive channels emerges from multimodal Vision-Language Models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) paired with autonomous browser automation. If an agent executes:

await page.screenshot({ path: 'viewport.png' });

all underlying DOM scrambles, font-table permutations, and tokenizer splitters are bypassed. The VLM simply applies Optical Character Recognition (OCR) or Vision Transformer (ViT) patch attention directly across the 2D raster image:

\[I_{\text{screenshot}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}\]

Can we prevent a static screenshot from conveying readable text to an AI, while keeping it completely readable to a human viewer?

The answer lies in human psychophysics and temporal visual integration.

6.2 Biological Critical Flicker Fusion (CFF) vs. Instantaneous Sampling

The human visual system does not perceive reality as a sequence of independent, isolated snapshots. Photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) and post-retinal ganglion cells exhibit a biological latency known as the persistence of vision, characterized by the Critical Flicker Fusion (CFF) threshold ($\approx 50\text{–}75\text{ Hz}$):

\[\text{Human Perceptual Integration: } I_{\text{human}}(x, y) = \int_{t - \tau}^{t} \mathcal{F}(x, y, t') \, dt' \quad (\tau \approx 60\text{ ms})\]

In contrast, a headless screenshot or camera capture samples the display buffer at a single discrete temporal instant:

\[\text{Machine Snapshot: } I_{\text{AI}}(x, y) = \mathcal{F}(x, y, t_0)\]

We can exploit this mathematical gap through three distinct perceptual techniques:

Method A: Sub-Frame Time-Division Multiplexing

We decompose every glyph outline into $K = 3$ to $5$ disjoint spatial sub-dot matrices. At $60\text{ Hz}$, the webpage alternates between these sub-matrices while simultaneously injecting uniformly distributed random noise dots in the background:

  • In any single frame $t_0$ (Screenshot): The density of dots inside the glyph matches the density of the random noise background. The mutual information $I(\text{Glyph}; \mathcal{F}(\cdot, t_0)) \approx 0$. OCR models and Vision Transformers see only uniform noise.
  • Over $60\text{ ms}$ (Human Eye): The human visual cortex integrates the alternating frames over time, perceiving crisp, continuous letterforms floating seamlessly above a faint gray backdrop.

Method B: Kinetic Counter-Phase Random-Dot Kinematograms (RDK)

Pioneered in visual neuroscience by Béla Julesz [3], an RDK renders foreground text and background using identical random dot distributions.

  • Background dots drift continuously to the right at speed $+v$.
  • Foreground text dots drift to the left at speed $-v$.
  • In any frozen screenshot, the spatial statistics of foreground and background are identically distributed ($D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{text}} \parallel P_{\text{bg}}) = 0$), rendering it mathematically impossible for any static image model to segment the text.
  • In motion, biological motion detectors in visual area V5/MT immediately separate the text from the background based on velocity contrast.

Interactive Laboratory 4: Live Anti-Screenshot Vault

Observe the live canvas below running at $60\text{ Hz}$. Notice how your eyes easily read the moving message. Then click “Simulate Screenshot (Freeze Single Frame)” to see what an AI vision model or screenshot crawler captures:

Lab 4: Anti-Screenshot Temporal Multiplexing & Kinetic RDK Vault

Tier 4 Defense
Refresh: 60 FPS Canvas Buffer Biological Integration Window: $\tau \approx 65\text{ ms}$

7. Comparative Defense Matrix & Architectural Synthesis

When deploying a Human-Exclusive Information Channel in production, defenses should be stacked in depth according to the threat profile:

Defensive Layer Implementation Mechanism Protects Against Human Friction Failure Boundary
Tier 1: Client PoW SHA-256 Hashcash + AES-256-GCM Raw HTTP Crawlers, Curl, GPTBot 0 ms perceived (runs in WebWorker) Headless browser running full V8 engine
Tier 2: Glyph Permutation Custom Dynamic WOFF2 cmap + Copy Trap Headless DOM Scrapers, Copy-Paste to ChatGPT Zero (standard vector typography) Full viewport raster screenshot + OCR
Tier 3: BPE Splitting Zero-width codepoints + Cyrillic homoglyphs Embedding Search, RAG Ingestion, Model Weights Zero (invisible rendering width) Rule-based Unicode normalization preprocessors
Tier 4: Temporal Multiplexing 60Hz canvas sub-frame temporal integration & RDK Static Screenshots, Vision-LLMs, OCR Scrapers Low (requires continuous visual stream) Multi-frame 60 FPS video stream capture

8. Open Questions & Future Horizons

Constructing information channels that are accessible to biological eyes yet opaque to artificial intelligence defines one of the most intellectually compelling frontiers in modern computer science. As multimodal models transition from processing static images to analyzing high-frame-rate continuous video streams with spatio-temporal attention, the boundary between biological perception and machine cognition will narrow further.

Key open challenges include:

  1. Accessibility Standards: How can human-exclusive channels maintain strict compliance with WCAG screen-reader accessibility for visually impaired humans without inadvertently presenting clean plaintext codepoints to automated AI crawlers?
  2. Ephemeral Neural Key Exchange: Could future client-side channels utilize eye-tracking micro-saccades or human cognitive response times as a biometric Proof-of-Humanity key derivation function?
  3. Formal Verification: Establishing formal bounds on the minimum mutual information leakage $I(\text{Model}; \text{Payload})$ achievable under arbitrary automated preprocessing.

9. Academic References & Grounding Literature

The four defensive tiers synthesized in this treatise build upon seminal results across distributed systems, natural language processing security, typography, and visual psychophysics:

  1. [1] Proof-of-Work & Asymmetric Throttling:
    Back, A. (2002). Hashcash - A Denial of Service Counter-Measure. Technical Report.
    (Introduced computational partial pre-image proof-of-work to impose economic friction on bulk automated senders).
  2. [2] Subword & Tokenizer Adversarial Vulnerabilities:
    Boucher, N., Anderson, R., & Almeyda, I. (2022). Bad Characters: Imperceptible NLP Attacks. In IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), pp. 1987–2004.
    (Demonstrated that imperceptible zero-width codepoints and homoglyphs catastrophically disrupt modern subword tokenizers).
  3. [3] Psychophysics of Motion-Defined Perception:
    Julesz, B. (1971). Foundations of Cyclopean Perception. The University of Chicago Press.
    (Pioneered Random-Dot Kinematograms and proved that human cortical area V5/MT performs temporal integration to perceive shape from motion where static frames contain zero spatial correlation).
  4. [4] Adversarial Triggers in NLP:
    Wallace, E., Feng, S., Kandpal, N., Gardner, M., & Singh, S. (2019). Universal Adversarial Triggers for Attacking and Analyzing NLP. In EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, pp. 2153–2162.
  5. [5] Robustness & Perturbation Toolkits:
    Morris, J. X., Lifland, E., Yoo, J. Y., Grigsby, J., Jin, D., & Qi, Y. (2020). TextAttack: A Framework for Adversarial Attacks, Data Augmentation, and Adversarial Training in NLP. In EMNLP 2020, pp. 119–126.
  6. [6] Adversarial Typography & Glyph Perturbation:
    Xiao, C., Cheng, C., Zheng, W., & Dong, Y. (2018). FontCode: Embedding Information in Text Documents using Glyph Perturbation. ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH 2018), 37(4).
  7. [7] In-Browser Native Cryptography:
    W3C Web Cryptography Working Group. (2017). Web Cryptography API - W3C Recommendation. World Wide Web Consortium.

link.title: HAS-RL: Clinician-Configured Force Safety in Robotic Ultrasound (BSc Thesis)

entry.content:
HAS-RL: Human-Adaptive Safe Reinforcement Learning

Clinician-Configured Force Safety in Robotic Ultrasound Spinal Scanning

Bachelor of Science Thesis in Computer Science · Amirkabir University of Technology (Tehran Polytechnic)

Mohammad Hadi Niknam

Research Paper (English PDF) AUT Thesis (Persian PDF) Defense Slides Simulator & Code

Overview / نگاه کلی

English Version
Abstract

Robotic ultrasound (US) imaging promises to standardize diagnostic scanning and alleviate sonographer fatigue. However, any robotic manipulator operating in direct physical contact with human anatomy must rigorously respect hard force-safety limits that vary across patients, tissue types, and clinician preferences. Prior safe reinforcement learning (RL) methods in robotic ultrasound train policies against a single, static force threshold; any change in tolerated force requires expensive retraining from scratch. Furthermore, recent multi-armed bandit multiplier methods designed for offline RL introduce destabilizing non-stationarity when transplanted into online policy-gradient loops.

We introduce HAS-RL (Human-Adaptive Safe Reinforcement Learning), a framework delivering: (i) Operator-Conditioned Zero-Shot Safety where the runtime safety ceiling κ is an observation state feature, tracking mid-scan dial adjustments without retraining or violations; (ii) Smoothed Bandit-Lagrangian (SBL) which applies an exponential moving average to EXP3 multiplier expectations to stabilize online learning; (iii) Anticipatory Trajectory Tracking cutting RMS tracking error by 28%; and (iv) Two-Sided Acoustic-Window Safety [κlow, κhigh] matching acoustic coupling physics.

Read Full Paper (English)
نسخه فارسی (پایان‌نامه دانشگاه صنعتی امیرکبیر)
چکیده پایان‌نامه

تصویربرداری اولتراسوند رباتیک راهکاری نویدبخش برای استانداردسازی اسکن‌های تشخیصی و کاهش خستگی سونوگرافر است؛ با این حال، سامانه‌های رباتیک کمکی به دلیل تماس فیزیکی مستقیم با بدن بیمار، ملزم به رعایت قیود سخت‌گیرانه برای فشار ایمن هستند؛ مقداری که بسته به نوع بافت، شرایط بالینی و ترجیح پزشک تغییر می‌کند. روش‌های پیشین یادگیری تقویتی ایمن در اولتراسوند رباتیک، یک policy را بر اساس یک آستانه نیروی ثابت آموزش می‌دهند؛ از این رو با هر تغییر در حد مجاز، کل فرایند آموزش باید از ابتدا تکرار شود.

در این پایان‌نامه، چارچوب HAS-RL با چهار نوآوری اصلی معرفی می‌شود: ۱. تنظیم آنلاین فشار ایمنی به صورت زیروشات: سقف مجاز مستقیماً در بردار مشاهده قرار گرفته و مدل بدون نیاز به بازآموزی، تغییر آنلاین پیچ تنظیم فشار در حین اسکن را دنبال می‌کند؛ ۲. سازوکار لاگرانژ باندیتی هموارشده (SBL): پایدارسازی متغیر دوگان باندیتی با میانگین متحرک نمایی؛ ۳. رهگیری مسیر پیش‌بین: کاهش ۲۸ درصدی خطای رهگیری؛ ۴. ایمنی پنجره آکوستیک دوطرفه: مدل‌سازی پنجره بالینی [κlow, κhigh].

دانلود پایان‌نامه کامل فارسی (۶۰ صفحه)

System Architecture / ساختار سیستم

The HAS-RL control pipeline bridges clinician inputs, reinforcement learning decision-making, and robotic compliance control.

Figure 1: Control loop and architecture of HAS-RL. The policy takes the state, anticipatory look-ahead error, and the operator's runtime safety limit κ to generate velocity actions under low-pass impedance contact dynamics.

Core Innovations / نوآوری‌های کلیدی

1. Operator-Conditioned Zero-Shot Safety / تنظیم آنلاین فشار زیروشات

Instead of baking a fixed $F_{\max}$ into policy weights, HAS-RL treats the clinician’s runtime safety setting as an observation variable: \(s_t = \left[x_t, y_t, F_t, e_t, \kappa_t\right]\)

The clinician can freely dial the force limit during an active scan. The policy reacts in real time, modulating contact force without a single constraint breach.

Figure 2: Mid-scan dial adjustment tracking. The policy tracks abrupt shifts in κ with 0 violations.
Figure 3: 7-point sweep across $[3, 12]\,\text{N}$. Contact force scales proportionally with zero breaches.

2. Smoothed Bandit-Lagrangian (SBL) / سازوکار لاگرانژ باندیتی هموارشده

To combine the bounded penalty guarantees of multi-armed bandit multiplier selection (EXP3) with online policy-gradient learning, SBL maintains an exponential moving average over expected multiplier weights: \(\bar{\lambda}_k = (1 - \tau)\bar{\lambda}_{k-1} + \tau \mathbb{E}_{a \sim p_k}[\lambda_a]\)

This resolves the gradient variance and policy collapse caused by raw bandit arm sampling while maintaining zero constraint violations.

3. Two-Sided Acoustic-Window Safety / پنجره ایمنی آکوستیک دوطرفه

Ultrasound imaging requires minimum contact to establish acoustic coupling, while excessive force injures soft tissue. HAS-RL enforces: \(\kappa_{\text{low}} \le F_{\text{contact}} \le \kappa_{\text{high}}\)

This eliminates the “headroom gap” of ceiling-only safety, reaching 10.2 N in $[9, 12]\,\text{N}$ windows versus 7.97 N under naive ceiling constraints.

Quantitative Evaluation / نتایج تجربی

Safety Performance Comparison ($\kappa = 5\,\text{N}$)

Method Mean Contact Force Max Force Image Quality Violations Safety Status
Vanilla PPO (Baseline) 5.23 N 5.48 N 0.90 95 Failed
HAS-RL (Ours) 3.62 N 3.77 N 0.47 0 100% Compliant

Multiplier-Mode Stability Ablation (3 Random Seeds)

Mode Mean Image Quality Train Violation Std ($\sigma_V$) Multiplier Std ($\sigma_\lambda$)
PPO-Lagrangian (Dual Ascent) 0.576 16.66 0.29
EXP3 Raw Bandit 0.492 13.51 1.43
Smoothed Bandit-Lagrangian (SBL - Ours) 0.603 11.99 0.42

Two-Sided Operator Window Performance

Clinician Window Mean Force In-Window Residence Violations Image Quality
$[2.5, 4.0]\,\text{N}$ 3.26 N 100% 0 0.67
$[5.0, 8.0]\,\text{N}$ 6.50 N 100% 0 0.99
$[9.0, 12.0]\,\text{N}$ 10.22 N 100% 0 0.74

Ultrasound B-Mode Image Reconstruction

HAS-RL Reconstruction: High acoustic fidelity maintained with strictly controlled force.
Baseline Reconstruction: Unconstrained force causing continuous safety breaches.

Amirkabir University of Technology Defense Details / جزئیات دفاع

  • عنوان پایان‌نامه: یادگیری تقویتی ایمن با تنظیم نیروی اپراتور در اسکن رباتیک اولتراسوند ستون فقرات
  • دانشگاه: دانشگاه صنعتی امیرکبیر (پلی‌تکنیک تهران) - دانشکده ریاضی و علوم کامپیوتر
  • مقطع و رشته: کارشناسی علوم کامپیوتر
  • نگارش: محمدهادی نیکنام
  • زمان دفاع: تابستان ۱۴۰۵
  • تعداد صفحات: ۶۰ صفحه به همراه اثبات‌های ریاضی و کدهای شبیه‌ساز

entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```
